questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kossel-Lewis approach to chemical bond formation
questions.question: In which of the following molecules does the central atom have an incomplete octet?

solution.key_concept: Incomplete octet is a limitation of the octet rule. In $BF_3$, boron has only 6 valence electrons.
steps: Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms three single bonds with F.
This gives 6 electrons around B, which is less than an octet.
N in $NH_3$, C in $CH_4$ and O in $H_2O$ all have 8 electrons around them.
solution.why_not_others: $NH_3$, $CH_4$ and $H_2O$ all obey the octet rule around the central atom.
solution.common_trap: Counting only bond pairs and ignoring lone pairs. N in $NH_3$ has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, which completes 8 electrons.
solution.time_saving_tip: Group 13 central atoms with three single bonds ($BF_3$, $BCl_3$) always have 6 electrons.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kossel-Lewis approach to chemical bond formation
questions.question: What is the formal charge on the oxygen atom in the hydronium ion, $H_3O^+$?

solution.key_concept: Formal charge is given by $FC = V - L - \frac{1}{2}S$.
steps: Oxygen has V = 6 valence electrons.
In $H_3O^+$, O has one lone pair, so L = 2.
O forms three O–H bonds, so S = 6.
solution.why_not_others: 0 assumes O is neutral as in water. $-1$ is a sign error. $-2$ comes from not halving the shared electrons: $6 - 2 - 6 = -2$.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to take only half of the shared electrons.
solution.time_saving_tip: An atom with one more bond than its usual valence (O with 3 bonds) carries a formal charge of +1.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kossel-Lewis approach to chemical bond formation
questions.question: Which of the following pairs consists only of odd-electron molecules?

solution.key_concept: Odd-electron molecules have an odd total number of valence electrons, so the octet cannot be satisfied for every atom.
steps: $NO$ has 5 + 6 = 11 valence electrons, which is odd.
$NO_2$ has 5 + 12 = 17 valence electrons, which is odd.
$CO$ has 10, $SO_2$ has 18 and $N_2O$ has 16 valence electrons, all even.
solution.why_not_others: Each of the other pairs contains at least one even-electron molecule: $CO$, $SO_2$ or $N_2O$.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every nitrogen oxide is odd-electron. $N_2O$ has 16 valence electrons.
solution.time_saving_tip: Add up the valence electrons. An odd total means an odd-electron molecule.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kossel-Lewis approach to chemical bond formation
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Noble gases are completely inert and do not form any compounds.
statements.R: Noble gases have a stable octet (a duplet in the case of helium) in their valence shell.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Noble gases do form compounds such as $XeF_2$ and $XeF_4$. This is one of the limitations of the octet rule.
steps: Xenon forms compounds such as $XeF_2$ and $XeF_4$, so A is false.
Noble gases do have a filled octet (duplet for He), so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) cannot be correct.
solution.common_trap: Equating a stable octet with complete chemical inertness.
solution.time_saving_tip: Recall $XeF_2$ and $XeF_4$ as direct counterexamples to noble gas inertness.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kossel-Lewis approach to chemical bond formation
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The formal charge on an atom in a molecule represents the actual charge present on that atom.
statements.II: In $IF_7$, the central iodine atom has 14 electrons in its valence shell, which is an example of an expanded octet.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Formal charge is only a bookkeeping charge. Expanded octets occur in $PF_5$ (10 electrons), $SF_6$ (12 electrons) and $IF_7$ (14 electrons).
steps: Formal charge does not represent the real charge on an atom, so Statement I is incorrect.
I forms 7 bonds in $IF_7$, giving 7 × 2 = 14 electrons around it, so Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, so options (1), (2) and (3) do not fit.
solution.common_trap: Treating formal charge as a real charge, or assuming 12 electrons is the maximum, as in $SF_6$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Electrons around a central atom with only single bonds and no lone pairs = 2 × number of bonds.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Formation of ionic bonds and factors affecting it
questions.question: Which of the following factors favours the formation of an ionic bond?
options: High ionisation enthalpy of the metal
Positive electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal
Low lattice enthalpy of the compound formed
Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal

solution.key_concept: Ionic bonding is favoured by low ionisation enthalpy of the metal, highly negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal and high lattice enthalpy.
steps: A metal with low ionisation enthalpy forms a cation easily.
This favours ionic bond formation.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal
solution.why_not_others: High ionisation enthalpy makes cation formation difficult. A positive electron gain enthalpy disfavours anion formation. Low lattice enthalpy gives a less stable solid.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the required trends for ionisation enthalpy and lattice enthalpy.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Formation of ionic bonds and factors affecting it
questions.question: For a hypothetical ionic solid MX, the data (in kJ/mol) are: sublimation enthalpy of M = +100, ionisation enthalpy of M = +500, bond dissociation enthalpy of $X_2$ = +240, electron gain enthalpy of X = −350, and lattice enthalpy U = +800 (energy needed to separate the lattice). What is the enthalpy of formation of MX?

solution.key_concept: Born-Haber cycle: $\Delta_f H = \Delta_{sub}H + IE + \frac{1}{2}\Delta_{diss}H + \Delta_{eg}H - U$.
steps: Half of the dissociation enthalpy: $\frac{1}{2}(240) = 120$.
Sum of the endothermic steps: $100 + 500 + 120 = 720$.
solution.why_not_others: $-310$ uses the full dissociation enthalpy (240). $+1170$ adds U instead of subtracting it. $+270$ takes the electron gain enthalpy as +350.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that only half a mole of $X_2$ is needed per mole of MX.
solution.time_saving_tip: Add all the steps that need energy, then subtract the steps that release energy.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Formation of ionic bonds and factors affecting it
questions.question: The conversion $Na(g) + Cl(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g)$ is endothermic, yet the formation of solid NaCl is exothermic overall. This is mainly due to:
options: the large lattice enthalpy released when the gaseous ions pack into the crystal
the electron gain enthalpy of chlorine alone exceeding the ionisation enthalpy of sodium
the release of energy when both ions attain the octet configuration
the energy released during the sublimation of sodium

solution.key_concept: Lattice enthalpy, not the octet alone, is the real driving force for forming ionic solids.
steps: IE of Na (+495.8) plus $\Delta_{eg}H$ of Cl (−348.7) gives +147.1 kJ/mol, which is endothermic.
Packing the gaseous ions into the lattice releases a large amount of energy (788 kJ/mol).
This makes the overall process exothermic.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): the large lattice enthalpy released when the gaseous ions pack into the crystal
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) is false: 348.7 is less than 495.8. Option (3) is false: attaining the octet does not by itself release enough energy. Option (4) is false: sublimation absorbs energy.
solution.common_trap: Crediting the octet configuration as the energy source.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Formation of ionic bonds and factors affecting it
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: The process $Na(g) + Cl(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g)$ is endothermic.
statements.R: The energy released when chlorine gains an electron is greater in magnitude than the energy required to ionise sodium.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: IE of Na is +495.8 kJ/mol and $\Delta_{eg}H$ of Cl is −348.7 kJ/mol, so the net change is +147.1 kJ/mol.
steps: The net energy change is positive, so the process is endothermic and A is true.
348.7 is less than 495.8, so R is false. If R were true, the process would be exothermic.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so options (1), (2) and (4) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Believing chlorine's highly negative electron gain enthalpy outweighs the ionisation of sodium.
solution.time_saving_tip: Compare magnitudes: 495.8 is greater than 348.7.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Formation of ionic bonds and factors affecting it
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The attainment of an octet by $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$ is by itself sufficient to make the formation of solid NaCl from gaseous Na and Cl atoms energetically favourable.
statements.II: The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to ionic compound formation and is used to determine lattice enthalpy indirectly.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The ion-forming steps are endothermic. Lattice enthalpy makes the overall process favourable, and it is found using the Born-Haber cycle.
steps: Forming the gaseous ions needs +147.1 kJ/mol, so the octet alone does not make the process favourable. Statement I is incorrect.
The Born-Haber cycle is based on Hess's law. Lattice enthalpy cannot be measured directly and is obtained from it. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, so options (1), (2) and (3) do not fit.
solution.common_trap: Overrating the octet rule as the driving force for ionic bonding.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: The lattice enthalpy of an ionic compound is the energy:
options: released when one mole of the compound is formed from its elements in their standard states
required to convert one mole of the solid into its constituent gaseous atoms
required to completely separate one mole of the solid ionic compound into its gaseous constituent ions
released when one mole of the compound dissolves in water

solution.key_concept: Lattice enthalpy is the energy needed to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions. For NaCl it is +788 kJ/mol.
steps: The definition refers to gaseous ions, not atoms.
It is an energy required, so it is positive in this convention.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): required to completely separate one mole of the solid ionic compound into its gaseous constituent ions
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) defines enthalpy of formation. Option (2) gives atoms instead of ions. Option (4) describes enthalpy of solution.
solution.common_trap: Confusing gaseous atoms with gaseous ions.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct order of lattice enthalpy?

solution.key_concept: $U \propto \frac{z_+ z_-}{r_+ + r_-}$. Ionic charge has the larger effect, and smaller ions give higher U.
steps: MgO and CaO have charges of +2 and −2, so they have the highest values. $Mg^{2+}$ is smaller than $Ca^{2+}$, so MgO > CaO.
NaF and NaCl have charges of +1 and −1. $F^-$ is smaller than $Cl^-$, so NaF > NaCl.
Order: MgO > CaO > NaF > NaCl.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) is fully reversed. Option (2) places a 1:1 halide above the 2:2 oxides. Option (4) reverses the size effect in both pairs.
solution.common_trap: Thinking larger ions give larger lattice enthalpy.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rank by charge product first, then by size within each group.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Using $U \propto \frac{z_+ z_-}{r_+ + r_-}$, consider ionic compound AB (made of $A^+$ and $B^-$) with $r_+ + r_- = 300$ pm, and ionic compound CD (made of $C^{2+}$ and $D^{2-}$) with $r_+ + r_- = 200$ pm. What is the ratio of the lattice enthalpy of CD to that of AB?

solution.key_concept: Lattice enthalpy is proportional to the product of the ionic charges and inversely proportional to the interionic distance.
steps: For CD: $\frac{2 \times 2}{200} = \frac{4}{200}$.
For AB: $\frac{1 \times 1}{300} = \frac{1}{300}$.
Ratio = $\frac{4}{200} \times \frac{300}{1} = 6.0$.
solution.why_not_others: 1.5 ignores the charges. 2.67 inverts the distance ratio ($4 \times 200/300$). 3.0 uses the sum of the charges instead of their product.
solution.common_trap: Adding the ionic charges instead of multiplying them.
solution.time_saving_tip: Ratio = (charge product ratio) × (inverse distance ratio) = 4 × 1.5.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Alkali halide with the highest lattice enthalpy

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Alkali halide with the lowest lattice enthalpy

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Method used to determine lattice enthalpy

solution.key_concept: Smallest ions give the highest lattice enthalpy. Lattice enthalpy is obtained indirectly from the Born-Haber cycle.
steps: The lattice enthalpy of NaCl is +788 kJ/mol (A-I).
$Li^+$ and $F^-$ are the smallest ions, so LiF has the highest value (B-II).
$Cs^+$ and $I^-$ are the largest ions, so CsI has the lowest value (C-III).
Lattice enthalpy is found using the Born-Haber cycle (D-IV).
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) swaps LiF and CsI. Option (3) swaps the numerical value with the method. Option (4) swaps CsI with the Born-Haber cycle.
solution.common_trap: Assuming heavier ions give stronger lattices.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following statements about lattice enthalpy are correct?

statements.A: Lattice enthalpy increases as the interionic distance increases.
statements.B: A higher lattice enthalpy generally means a higher melting point and greater hardness.
statements.C: An ionic compound dissolves in water if its hydration enthalpy can compensate its lattice enthalpy.
statements.D: Lattice enthalpy can be measured directly by experiment.
statements.E: Lattice enthalpy is proportional to the product of the ionic charges.

solution.key_concept: $U \propto \frac{z_+ z_-}{r_+ + r_-}$. Lattice enthalpy governs melting point and hardness, and together with hydration enthalpy it governs solubility.
steps: A is false: U is inversely proportional to the interionic distance.
B is true: a strong lattice gives a high melting point and greater hardness.
C is true: solubility depends on hydration enthalpy compensating lattice enthalpy.
D is false: lattice enthalpy cannot be measured directly and is found from the Born-Haber cycle.
E is true: U is proportional to $z_+ z_-$.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): B, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) includes the false statement A. Options (2) and (3) include the false statement D.
solution.common_trap: Thinking lattice enthalpy is measured directly, like enthalpy of combustion.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rule out A and D first. Only one option contains neither of them.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following elements has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?

solution.key_concept: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, with a Pauling value of 4.0.
steps: Recall the Pauling values: F = 4.0, O = 3.5, N = Cl = 3.0.
The highest value belongs to fluorine.
solution.why_not_others: Oxygen (3.5) comes second. Nitrogen and chlorine are both 3.0.
solution.common_trap: Choosing chlorine because it has a high electron gain enthalpy. Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity are different properties.
solution.time_saving_tip: Memorise the order F > O > N = Cl > C > H.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: For a bond A–B, the bond energy exceeds the mean of the A–A and B–B bond energies by 25 kcal/mol. Using the Pauling relation, what is the electronegativity difference $(\chi_A - \chi_B)$?

solution.key_concept: Pauling relation: $\chi_A - \chi_B = 0.208\sqrt{\Delta}$, with $\Delta$ in kcal/mol.
steps: Here $\Delta = 25$ kcal/mol, so $\sqrt{\Delta} = 5$.
solution.why_not_others: 5.20 comes from forgetting the square root ($0.208 \times 25$). 0.52 comes from wrongly halving the result. 0.0083 comes from dividing 0.208 by 25.
solution.common_trap: Multiplying 0.208 by $\Delta$ directly instead of by $\sqrt{\Delta}$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Choose or spot perfect-square values of $\Delta$ and take the root first.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: What is the correct order of electronegativity of the carbon atoms in ethane, ethene and ethyne?

solution.key_concept: The electronegativity of carbon rises with s-character: $C_{sp} > C_{sp^2} > C_{sp^3}$.
steps: Ethyne carbon is $sp$ (50% s), ethene carbon is $sp^2$ (33% s) and ethane carbon is $sp^3$ (25% s).
More s-character means higher electronegativity, so ethyne > ethene > ethane.
solution.why_not_others: The first option reverses the trend. The third option misplaces the $sp$ carbon. The last option ignores the effect of hybridisation.
solution.common_trap: Assuming one element always has the same electronegativity regardless of hybridisation.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rank by percentage s-character: 50 > 33 > 25.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Electronegativity of an element is the measurable energy released when an electron is added to its isolated gaseous atom.
statements.R: Electronegativity is a relative property of an atom in a molecule and has no units.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Electronegativity concerns a bonded atom and has no units. Electron gain enthalpy is a measurable energy change of an isolated gaseous atom.
steps: A actually describes electron gain enthalpy, not electronegativity, so A is false.
R correctly states that electronegativity is a relative, unitless property of a bonded atom, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so the first three options, which all treat A as true, are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Treating electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy as the same property.
solution.time_saving_tip: Bonded atom means electronegativity. Isolated gaseous atom means electron gain enthalpy.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Oxygen is the second most electronegative element and has a Pauling electronegativity of 3.0.
statements.II: On the Pauling scale, a C–H bond is more polar than an H–Cl bond.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Pauling values are O = 3.5, N = Cl = 3.0, C = 2.5 and H = 2.1. Bond polarity depends on the electronegativity difference.
steps: Oxygen is indeed second, but its value is 3.5, not 3.0, so Statement I is incorrect.
For C–H, $\Delta\chi = 2.5 - 2.1 = 0.4$. For H–Cl, $\Delta\chi = 3.0 - 2.1 = 0.9$.
H–Cl has the larger difference and is more polar, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I gives the wrong value for oxygen (3.0 belongs to N and Cl). Statement II reverses the polarity order.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the value 3.0 (N, Cl) with 3.5 (O).
solution.time_saving_tip: Compute $\Delta\chi$ directly to compare bond polarity.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: According to Fajans' rule, which lithium halide has the maximum covalent character?

solution.key_concept: For the same cation, a larger anion is more polarisable, so the bond has more covalent character.
steps: The cation $Li^+$ is common to all four compounds.
Anion size increases in the order $F^- < Cl^- < Br^- < I^-$, so $I^-$ is the most polarisable.
Hence $LiI$ is the most covalent.
solution.why_not_others: $LiF$ is the least covalent because $F^-$ is the smallest anion. $LiCl$ and $LiBr$ are intermediate.
solution.common_trap: Picking $LiF$ because F is the most electronegative.
solution.time_saving_tip: Same cation: biggest anion gives the most covalent compound.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: What is the correct order of covalent character among $NaCl$, $MgCl_2$ and $AlCl_3$?

solution.key_concept: A smaller, more highly charged cation has greater polarising power and gives more covalent character.
steps: Going from $Na^+$ to $Mg^{2+}$ to $Al^{3+}$, the cation charge increases and its size decreases.
Polarising power is therefore highest for $Al^{3+}$.
Order of covalent character: $AlCl_3 > MgCl_2 > NaCl$.
solution.why_not_others: The first option is the reverse order. The third and fourth options break the steady trend in cation charge.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a higher cation charge makes a compound more ionic.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use the ionic potential $\phi = $ charge/radius; it increases from $Na^+$ to $Al^{3+}$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: $CuCl$ is more covalent than $NaCl$ even though $Cu^+$ and $Na^+$ have similar ionic sizes. What is the best reason for this?
options: $Cu^+$ has an 18-electron (pseudo noble gas) configuration whose poorly shielding d electrons make it more polarising
$Cu^+$ has an 8-electron noble gas configuration like $Na^+$ but a smaller radius
The chloride ion in $CuCl$ is larger than the chloride ion in $NaCl$

solution.key_concept: Cations with an 18-electron configuration are more polarising than noble gas cations of similar size.
steps: Both cations carry a +1 charge and have similar sizes.
The d electrons of $Cu^+$ shield the nuclear charge poorly, so its effective polarising power is higher.
It distorts $Cl^-$ more strongly, which gives $CuCl$ more covalent character.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): $Cu^+$ has an 18-electron (pseudo noble gas) configuration whose poorly shielding d electrons make it more polarising
solution.why_not_others: Both ions are +1, so charge is not the difference. $Cu^+$ is not an 8-electron ion, and the stem states the sizes are similar. The anion is $Cl^-$ in both compounds.
solution.common_trap: Looking only at size and charge and ignoring the electronic configuration of the cation.
solution.time_saving_tip: Treat $Cu^+$, $Ag^+$ and $Zn^{2+}$ as 18-electron cations that are extra polarising.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Smaller cation of the same charge, both noble gas type

solution.key_concept: Fajans' factors are cation size, cation charge, anion size and the 18-electron configuration of the cation.
steps: A: $Li^+$ is smaller than $Na^+$, and both are +1 noble gas ions, so A matches II.
B: $Cu^+$ is an 18-electron cation, so B matches III.
C: $I^-$ is larger than $F^-$, so C matches I.
D: $Al^{3+}$ carries a higher charge than $Na^+$, so D matches IV.
solution.why_not_others: The other options assign the charge factor or the 18-electron factor to pairs where it does not apply.
solution.common_trap: Attributing the extra covalency of $CuCl$ to cation size, even though $Cu^+$ and $Na^+$ are similar in size.
solution.time_saving_tip: Fix B (the only 18-electron cation) and C (the only change of anion) first.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Fajans' rule are correct?

statements.A: A higher ionic potential (charge/radius of the cation) means greater polarising power and more covalent character.
statements.B: Greater covalent character increases the solubility of a compound in water.
statements.C: $AgCl$ has a lower solubility in water than expected because of its covalent character.
statements.D: A larger anion is less polarisable than a smaller anion of the same charge.
statements.E: Greater covalent character raises the solubility of a compound in organic solvents.

solution.key_concept: Covalent character lowers melting point and water solubility and raises solubility in organic solvents. Larger anions are more polarisable.
steps: A is correct: a higher $\phi$ means greater polarising power.
B is incorrect: covalent character lowers water solubility.
C is correct: covalency makes $AgCl$ poorly soluble in water.
D is incorrect: larger anions are more polarisable.
E is correct: covalent compounds dissolve better in organic solvents.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Any option containing B or D includes a false statement. 'A and C only' leaves out the true statement E.
solution.common_trap: Believing that a larger anion holds its electron cloud more tightly.
solution.time_saving_tip: Eliminate B first, which removes one option at once.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following molecules has a non-zero dipole moment?

solution.key_concept: Symmetrical molecules have zero dipole moment because their bond dipoles cancel.
steps: $CO_2$ (linear), $BF_3$ (trigonal planar) and $CCl_4$ (tetrahedral) are symmetrical, so their dipoles cancel.
$H_2O$ is bent, so its bond dipoles do not cancel; its dipole moment is 1.85 D.
solution.why_not_others: $CO_2$, $BF_3$ and $CCl_4$ contain polar bonds but have zero net dipole moment because of their symmetry.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that polar bonds always make a polar molecule.
solution.time_saving_tip: Check the shape: a bent molecule with lone pairs on the central atom is polar.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: A diatomic molecule HX has an observed dipole moment of 1.6 D. Its dipole moment calculated for a fully ionic bond is 6.4 D. What is the percent ionic character of the H–X bond?

solution.key_concept: $\%$ ionic character $= \frac{\mu_{observed}}{\mu_{ionic}} \times 100$.
solution.why_not_others: 75% is the covalent fraction, not the ionic fraction. 2.5% comes from a decimal slip. 400% comes from inverting the ratio.
solution.common_trap: Dividing $\mu_{ionic}$ by $\mu_{observed}$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Percent ionic character can never exceed 100%, so 400% can be rejected at once.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: What is the correct order of dipole moment among $CH_3Cl$, $CH_2Cl_2$, $CHCl_3$ and $CCl_4$?

solution.key_concept: As more C–Cl bonds are added around the tetrahedral carbon, their dipoles increasingly cancel. $CCl_4$ has zero dipole moment.
steps: $CCl_4$ is perfectly symmetrical, so its dipole moment is zero.
The order is $CH_3Cl > CH_2Cl_2 > CHCl_3 > CCl_4$.
solution.why_not_others: The second option assumes that more Cl atoms give more polarity. The third and fourth options place $CHCl_3$ or $CCl_4$ wrongly.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that more electronegative atoms always give a larger dipole moment.
solution.time_saving_tip: Any option that does not place $CCl_4$ last is wrong.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: $XeF_2$ has a non-zero dipole moment because the central Xe atom carries three lone pairs.
statements.II: Considering dipole moment alone, ethanol has a higher dipole moment than acetone.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: A linear, symmetrical $XeF_2$ has zero dipole moment. By dipole moment alone, acetone (about 2.9 D) is higher than ethanol (about 1.7 D).
steps: In $XeF_2$ the three lone pairs sit in equatorial positions and the two F atoms are axial, so the molecule is linear and symmetrical. Its net dipole is zero, so Statement I is incorrect.
Acetone (about 2.9 D) has a higher dipole moment than ethanol (about 1.7 D), so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are false, so every other option fails.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the polarity order based on hydrogen bonding (ethanol above acetone) with the order of actual dipole moment values.
solution.time_saving_tip: Lone pairs placed symmetrically do not produce a net dipole.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hybridization involving s, p and d orbitals
questions.question: What is the hybridisation of sulphur in $SF_6$?

solution.key_concept: Six electron pairs around the central atom correspond to $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation, which is octahedral.
steps: S has 6 valence electrons and forms 6 S–F bonds.
A hybridisation number of 6 means $sp^3d^2$ (octahedral).
solution.why_not_others: $sp^3$ needs 4 pairs and $sp^3d$ needs 5 pairs. $dsp^2$ uses inner d orbitals and is square planar, as in $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$.
solution.common_trap: Confusing $sp^3d^2$ with $dsp^2$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hybridization involving s, p and d orbitals
questions.question: Using $H = \frac{1}{2}(V + M - c + a)$, what is the hybridisation of chlorine in $ClF_3$?

solution.key_concept: The hybridisation number counts both bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom.
steps: V = 7 for Cl and M = 3 for the three F atoms. The species is neutral, so c = a = 0.
A hybridisation number of 5 means $sp^3d$. The two lone pairs sit in equatorial positions, giving a T shape.
solution.why_not_others: $sp^2$ counts only the three bonds and ignores the lone pairs. $sp^3$ and $sp^3d^2$ come from arithmetic errors in counting electron pairs.
solution.common_trap: Deducing trigonal planar $sp^2$ from the three F atoms alone.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hybridization involving s, p and d orbitals
questions.question: What is the percentage s-character of the carbon hybrid orbitals in $C_2H_2$, $C_2H_4$ and $CH_4$, respectively?

solution.key_concept: $\%\,s = \frac{1}{\text{number of orbitals mixed}} \times 100$
steps: In $C_2H_2$ carbon is sp, so s-character = 1/2 = 50%.
In $C_2H_4$ carbon is $sp^2$, so s-character = 1/3 = 33.3%.
In $CH_4$ carbon is $sp^3$, so s-character = 1/4 = 25%.
solution.why_not_others: The other options reverse or shuffle the sp, $sp^2$ and $sp^3$ values.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that more mixed orbitals means more s-character.
solution.time_saving_tip: s-character is simply 1 divided by the number of orbitals mixed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hybridization involving s, p and d orbitals
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: The hybridisation follows from the number of electron pairs. Square planar complexes such as $[PtCl_4]^{2-}$ are $dsp^2$.
steps: $PCl_5$ has 5 pairs, so it is $sp^3d$ (III).
$SF_6$ has 6 pairs, so it is $sp^3d^2$ (IV).
$IF_7$ has 7 pairs, so it is $sp^3d^3$ (I).
$[PtCl_4]^{2-}$ is square planar, so it is $dsp^2$ (II).
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps $PCl_5$ and $SF_6$. Option 2 swaps $IF_7$ and the Pt complex. Option 4 swaps $PCl_5$ and $IF_7$.
solution.common_trap: Assigning $sp^3$ or $sp^3d^2$ to the square planar $[PtCl_4]^{2-}$ instead of $dsp^2$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Hybridization involving s, p and d orbitals
questions.question: Which of the following statements about hybridisation are correct?

statements.A: In $PCl_5$, the axial P–Cl bonds are longer and weaker than the equatorial P–Cl bonds.
statements.B: Hybrid orbitals can form pi bonds as well as sigma bonds.
statements.C: $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is $sp^3$ tetrahedral, whereas $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is $dsp^2$ square planar.
statements.D: Only half-filled atomic orbitals can take part in hybridisation.

solution.key_concept: Hybrid orbitals form only sigma bonds or hold lone pairs. Both half-filled and fully filled orbitals can hybridise.
steps: A is correct: in $sp^3d$ $PCl_5$, the axial bonds are longer and weaker.
B is incorrect: pi bonds use unhybridised orbitals.
C is correct: the two Ni complexes have different geometries.
D is incorrect: fully filled orbitals can also hybridise.
E is correct: solid $PCl_5$ is ionic, $[PCl_4]^+[PCl_6]^-$.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes B or D, and both of these are false.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that only half-filled orbitals hybridise, or that all $[NiX_4]^{2-}$ complexes share one geometry.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rule out B and D first. Only one option is then left.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: What is the average C–O bond order in the carbonate ion, $CO_3^{2-}$?

solution.key_concept: B.O. = total bonds between the two atom types ÷ number of resonating structures.
steps: Each canonical form has one C=O and two C–O bonds, so there are 4 bonds in total between C and O.
There are 3 resonating positions.
solution.why_not_others: 1 and 2 are the bond orders in a single canonical form. 1.5 applies to two-position systems such as $O_3$.
solution.common_trap: Using 1.5 for every resonating oxyanion.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: In ozone, the O–O single bond length is 148 pm and the O=O double bond length is 121 pm. What are the two O–O bond lengths in $O_3$?
options: One is 121 pm and the other is 148 pm

solution.key_concept: Resonance averages bond lengths. The hybrid has equal bonds of intermediate length.
steps: $O_3$ is a resonance hybrid of two canonical forms.
Both O–O bonds become equal, with bond order 1.5.
Their length, 128 pm, lies between 148 pm and 121 pm.
solution.why_not_others: Option 3 describes a single canonical form, which has no real existence. Options 1 and 2 ignore resonance completely.
solution.common_trap: Treating one canonical form as the real structure.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: In which species is the average X–O bond order (X = central atom) equal to 1.25?

solution.key_concept: Average bond order = total bonds ÷ number of resonating positions.
steps: $PO_4^{3-}$ has 5 P–O bonds spread over 4 positions, so B.O. = 5/4 = 1.25.
$SO_4^{2-}$ has B.O. = 1.5, with d-orbital participation.
solution.why_not_others: $SO_4^{2-}$ and $NO_2^-$ give 1.5, and $NO_3^-$ gives 1.33.
solution.common_trap: Assuming $SO_4^{2-}$ and $PO_4^{3-}$ have the same bond order because both are tetrahedral oxyanions.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: All the C–C bonds in benzene have the same length, 139 pm.
statements.R: Resonance averages the bond lengths, so every C–C bond in benzene has a bond order of 1.5.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Resonance averages bond orders and bond lengths.
steps: Benzene is a resonance hybrid, and all its C–C bonds are 139 pm.
Averaging alternating single and double bonds gives bond order 1.5 for every C–C bond.
Equal bond orders lead to equal bond lengths, so R explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, and the averaging in R is the direct cause of the equal lengths in A.
solution.common_trap: Picturing benzene as alternating single and double bonds of different lengths.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In the formate ion, $HCOO^-$, both C–O bonds have a bond order of 1.5.
statements.II: The energy difference between the actual molecule and its most stable canonical form is called the resonance energy.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Resonance gives equal averaged bonds, and resonance energy measures the extra stability of the hybrid.
steps: In $HCOO^-$ there are 3 bonds between C and the two O atoms, spread over 2 positions, so B.O. = 1.5. Statement I is correct.
Resonance energy is defined as the energy difference between the actual molecule and its most stable canonical form. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements agree with the definitions and the bond order calculation.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that formate has one C=O and one C–O bond of different orders.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Bonding and antibonding orbitals; sigma and pi bonds
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes an antibonding molecular orbital?
options: It concentrates electron density between the two nuclei
It has a nodal plane between the nuclei and lies higher in energy than the parent atomic orbitals
It is formed by constructive overlap of the atomic orbitals
It lies lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals and stabilises the molecule

solution.key_concept: Antibonding MOs come from destructive overlap. They have a node between the nuclei and lie higher in energy than the parent AOs.
steps: Destructive overlap cancels electron density between the nuclei, which creates a nodal plane there.
With no density between the nuclei, repulsion is not reduced, so the orbital lies above the parent AOs.
Electrons in it destabilise the molecule.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): It has a nodal plane between the nuclei and lies higher in energy than the parent atomic orbitals
solution.why_not_others: Options 1, 3 and 4 describe a bonding MO: electron density between the nuclei, constructive overlap and lower energy.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the features of bonding and antibonding orbitals.
solution.time_saving_tip: An asterisk (*) means a node between the nuclei and higher energy.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Bonding and antibonding orbitals; sigma and pi bonds
questions.question: Which molecular orbital has a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis and also an additional node between the nuclei?

solution.key_concept: All pi MOs have a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis. $\pi^*$ orbitals also have an additional node between the nuclei.
steps: A nodal plane containing the internuclear axis is the mark of a pi orbital, so the choice is between $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi^* 2p_x$.
An extra node between the nuclei is the mark of an antibonding orbital.
Only $\pi^* 2p_x$ has both features.
solution.why_not_others: $\sigma 2p_z$ is symmetrical about the axis and has no node between the nuclei. $\pi 2p_x$ has no node between the nuclei. $\sigma^* 2p_z$ has a node between the nuclei but is cylindrically symmetrical, so no nodal plane contains the axis.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $\sigma^* 2p_z$ because it is antibonding, while forgetting that sigma orbitals have no nodal plane containing the axis.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Bonding and antibonding orbitals; sigma and pi bonds
questions.question: When two atomic orbitals combine to form a bonding and an antibonding molecular orbital, which statement about their energies is correct?
options: The bonding MO is lowered by exactly the same amount as the antibonding MO is raised
The antibonding MO is raised slightly more than the bonding MO is lowered
The bonding MO is lowered more than the antibonding MO is raised
Both the bonding and antibonding MOs lie below the parent atomic orbitals

solution.key_concept: Energy splitting is unequal: the antibonding MO is destabilised slightly more than the bonding MO is stabilised.
steps: The bonding MO lies below the parent AOs.
The antibonding MO lies above the parent AOs.
The rise of the antibonding MO is slightly larger than the fall of the bonding MO.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): The antibonding MO is raised slightly more than the bonding MO is lowered
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 assumes symmetric splitting. Option 3 reverses the asymmetry. Option 4 is wrong because the antibonding MO lies above the parent AOs.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the splitting is symmetric.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Bonding and antibonding orbitals; sigma and pi bonds
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: An electron placed in the $\sigma^* 1s$ orbital destabilises the molecule.
statements.R: The $\sigma^* 1s$ orbital is symmetrical about the internuclear axis.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Antibonding electrons destabilise a molecule because the orbital lies higher in energy and has a node between the nuclei, not because of its symmetry.
steps: $\sigma^* 1s$ is an antibonding MO, higher in energy than the 1s AOs, so A is true.
All sigma MOs, bonding or antibonding, are symmetrical about the internuclear axis, so R is true.
The bonding $\sigma 1s$ orbital has the same symmetry, so symmetry cannot explain destabilisation. R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R is a true statement, so options 3 and 4 fail. R does not explain A, so option 1 fails.
solution.common_trap: Accepting any true reason as the explanation.
solution.time_saving_tip: Ask whether R would also apply to the bonding orbital. If it would, it cannot explain destabilisation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Bonding and antibonding orbitals; sigma and pi bonds
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The $\sigma 2p_z$ molecular orbital has a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis.
statements.II: Electrons in a bonding molecular orbital increase internuclear repulsion and therefore destabilise the molecule.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Sigma MOs are cylindrically symmetrical about the internuclear axis. Bonding MOs place electron density between the nuclei, which reduces repulsion and stabilises the molecule.
steps: A nodal plane containing the internuclear axis is a feature of pi MOs. $\sigma 2p_z$ is symmetrical about the axis, so Statement I is incorrect.
Bonding MOs concentrate electron density between the nuclei, which reduces repulsion and lowers energy, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I describes a pi orbital, not a sigma orbital. Statement II describes the opposite of what bonding electrons do.
solution.common_trap: Assuming any p-derived MO must have a nodal plane along the axis.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following compounds shows intramolecular hydrogen bonding?

solution.key_concept: An intramolecular hydrogen bond forms within a single molecule. It occurs when the H-bond donor and the acceptor are close together, as in o-nitrophenol and salicylaldehyde.
steps: In o-nitrophenol, the $-OH$ and $-NO_2$ groups sit on adjacent carbons.
The H of $-OH$ therefore bonds to an O of the $-NO_2$ group in the same molecule, which forms a chelate ring.
p-Nitrophenol, acetic acid and ethanol all form hydrogen bonds between different molecules (intermolecular).
solution.why_not_others: In p-nitrophenol the groups are too far apart, so it bonds intermolecularly. Acetic acid forms intermolecular dimers in benzene. Ethanol molecules H-bond with one another.
solution.common_trap: The acetic acid dimer is a cyclic H-bonded structure, and this tempts students to call it intramolecular. It is actually intermolecular because two separate molecules are joined.
solution.time_saving_tip: Look for an ortho arrangement of an $-OH$ group next to an acceptor group. That pattern signals intramolecular H-bonding.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: The correct order of boiling points of $H_2O$, $HF$ and $NH_3$ is:

solution.key_concept: Boiling point depends on the total extent of hydrogen bonding per molecule, and not only on the strength of a single H-bond.
steps: The F–H···F bond is the strongest individual hydrogen bond.
However, each $H_2O$ molecule forms more hydrogen bonds than an $HF$ molecule does.
As a result, water has the most extensive H-bond network and the highest boiling point.
$NH_3$ has the weakest N–H···N bonds and the lowest boiling point, so the order is $H_2O > HF > NH_3$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) ranks the compounds only by single H-bond strength. Option (2) reverses the true order. Option (4) wrongly places $NH_3$ above $HF$.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that $HF$ boils highest because the F–H···F bond is the strongest individual H-bond.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember that water is anomalous because it forms more H-bonds per molecule.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Ice floats on liquid water because:
options: ice has a closely packed structure in which molecules are held by covalent bonds
intramolecular hydrogen bonding in ice reduces its mass
hydrogen bonding in ice produces an open cage structure with empty spaces
hydrogen bonds are absent in ice but present in liquid water

solution.key_concept: In ice, intermolecular hydrogen bonding arranges water molecules into an open cage structure.
steps: In ice, each water molecule is held in a fixed position by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
This arrangement produces an open cage structure that contains empty spaces.
Ice therefore occupies a larger volume than the same mass of liquid water.
Its density is lower, so ice floats on water.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): hydrogen bonding in ice produces an open cage structure with empty spaces
solution.why_not_others: Ice is not closely packed, and the forces holding its molecules together are H-bonds, not covalent bonds. The H-bonding in ice is intermolecular, and bonding cannot change mass anyway. Hydrogen bonds are present in ice.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a solid is always denser than its liquid.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: p-Nitrophenol is steam volatile whereas o-nitrophenol is not.
statements.R: o-Nitrophenol shows intramolecular hydrogen bonding while p-nitrophenol shows intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Intramolecular H-bonding lowers boiling point and makes a compound volatile. Intermolecular H-bonding associates molecules together and raises boiling point.
steps: o-Nitrophenol forms intramolecular H-bonds (chelation), so its molecules are not associated with each other.
p-Nitrophenol forms intermolecular H-bonds, so its molecules are associated and its boiling point is higher.
Hence o-nitrophenol is the steam volatile one and p-nitrophenol is not, which makes A false.
R correctly describes the type of H-bonding in each isomer, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A swaps the two isomers, so any option that treats A as true is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that intramolecular hydrogen bonding raises boiling point.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use the link ortho, then chelation, then volatile.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The strength of hydrogen bonds follows the order N–H···N > O–H···O > F–H···F.
statements.II: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding in salicylaldehyde increases its boiling point and its solubility in water.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Hydrogen bond strength increases with the electronegativity of the atom involved. Intramolecular H-bonding reduces both boiling point and water solubility.
steps: The correct strength order is F–H···F > O–H···O > N–H···N. Statement I gives the reverse order, so it is incorrect.
In salicylaldehyde, the intramolecular H-bond causes chelation.
Chelation reduces association between molecules and reduces H-bonding with water.
This lowers the boiling point and the water solubility, so Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I reverses the strength order, and Statement II reverses the effect of intramolecular H-bonding. Any option that marks either statement as correct is therefore wrong.
solution.common_trap: Treating every kind of hydrogen bond as something that raises boiling point and solubility, without separating intermolecular from intramolecular bonding.
solution.time_saving_tip: Both statements are reversals of standard facts. Check the direction of each claim first.
